segments.name: LinkedIn About (long bio)
segments.text:
I've spent my career in live events and production. Straight out of uni I joined the top end of the Australian industry as a junior video editor, and five years later I was General Manager. I've delivered over 115 live events for more than 56,000 attendees, and I've managed multimillion dollar budgets.

In five years with Aaron Sansoni, I learned how to grow businesses. Now I partner with founders in live events and production. I help grow businesses through new ventures, partnerships, products and optimisation. Partnering or investing, and giving you the option to exit.

Relationships carry this industry. I've built mine across every discipline, project managers, AV providers, manufacturers, venues, and talent. When something needs to happen fast, I'm calling someone I know.

My goal is to be in business with, or partnered into, every area of live events and production.

If you own a live events or production business and want to talk about what's next, reach out.
segments.note: Approved July 2026. The reference for all long bios. Ryan wrote the final structure himself.

segments.name: Official statement (said in every video)
segments.text: Most event businesses try to do everything themselves. Their own AV, their own crew, their own venue if they can swing it. It protects the margin and caps everything else, because nobody is the best at all of it. I believe you grow faster by partnering with people who are the best at their piece. You give up a clip of the ticket. You get back quality, reputation, and the time to be great at the thing you're actually great at.
segments.note: The Partnership Belief System opener. Reintroduce it every video, word for word.

segments.note: The causality is deliberate. Never shorten it to a supplier says no, a partner says yes. Never chained with the keeper line.

gold.name: China Post 1 · the network
gold.text:
I'm in 🇨🇳China this week, visiting the factories that manufacture the equipment we use in live events and production.

Everything I came here to purchase, I could've ordered from Alibaba or direct from a distributor in Aus.

But the gear was only half the reason for the trip. I wanted to meet the people behind the businesses.

So far I've walked the production lines, watched gear get assembled and QC tested, and sat down for lunch with the teams I could be working with for the rest of my life. We talked holidays, hobbies, nerdy shit we like. Not just products and specs.

A few of these factories manufacture for the biggest brands in our industry, and for Aussie distributors I already work with. So every relationship I build here strengthens my connections across the industry.

The play is the network. I'm building direct relationships across every discipline of production and events. Staging, Truss, Lighting, LED, Audio. So when I, someone I work with, or a future venture needs good equipment, I'm not starting from scratch. I'm calling someone I've had lunch with.

This is exactly how I operate in Australia. Equipment rental, contractors, emergency situations! The people I call first are the ones I've got relationships with, and it never lets me down. No reason that stops at the border. So I'm extending it to the manufacturers themselves.

Worth every hour.
gold.why: In the moment narration, contrast set early with Alibaba, a long Provost sentence carrying real detail, the principle lands after the story proves it, one dry punch close.

gold.name: China Post 2 · the masterclass
gold.text:
I walked into a factory in 🇨🇳China last week as a brand new lead. No orders, and no history.

They spent over 8 hours with us, and never pushed a sale or contract.

A welcome tea, demo show, product walk thoughts, a catered lunch with their team, full factory tour, and a project meeting to meet our needs not theirs (and in one case a guided tour through their very own lighting museum). Never any rush, and no pressure.

In live production the job IS the experience we create for people. So I notice when someone does it well. This was a masterclass in how to treat a potential customer, they literally turned a sales meeting into a live experience.

And it works I walked out thinking about long term business with them.

Plenty of businesses in Australia could take notes.
gold.why: Tension in two lines, the detail list is the story, one principle paragraph connecting to craft identity, dry Australian punch close. The flag emoji is the only sanctioned emoji use, one functional visual flag.

gold.name: The angle of a table · Personal
gold.text:
Early in my career, Aaron Sansoni taught me something over the angle of a table that I still use on every event.

I was still a junior. We were about 30 minutes from doors, and the room was 95% there. I'd looked at this wing of tables, thought it wasn't quite perfect, but decided it was close enough, and moved on.

Aaron walked the room and stopped at it. He told me why it mattered, and made it clear that holding the standard was my job no matter how small the thing was. With nowhere near enough time, we adjusted just about the whole room.

What I learned that day was to hold my own standard even when it's inconvenient, for me or for the team. The little things are the first to drop when bigger things are going wrong. Drop them once and that becomes the standard next time. I see it all over our industry, people getting by on putting an event on instead of putting on the best experience they possibly can.

Since then there have been plenty of times I've pulled up something small and been told it isn't the priority right now, or told myself the same thing. Now I think, who's going to trust me with something bigger if I let this slip because it's easy and close enough?
gold.why: The reference Personal post. One small physical object carries the whole piece, exact numbers, a real admission, Aaron in past tense lesson framing only, and a callback close that turns a discipline story into a partner room signal without pitching.
